newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Amnesty gears up for campaign at UN rights forum.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty gears up for campaign at UN rights forum.

text.p: Amnesty International accused the United States and European Union on Thursday of protecting violators from scrutiny by the U.N. Human Rights Commission -- including China, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia and Turkey.

China will likely escape censure for the seventh year running at the United Nations forum, which opens on Monday, because Washington and Brussels have been lax in lobbying for support for a resolution, according to Amnesty delegates.
The London-based group named five states for top scrutiny at the forum, alleging their security forces tortured and killed civilians. The five were Algeria, Colombia, Indonesia, Nigeria and Turkey.
Amnesty called for reform in the main U.N. human rights body whose 53 member states hold their six-week session in Geneva.
"The message is: trade and human rights are linked," Nicholas Howen, Amnesty's legal director, said at a news briefing in Geneva.

"We see a range of 'untouchables' -- countries that won't be touched, even though there are severe human rights violations, because of the economic and political interests of the big powers and others in the Commission," he added.

Allegations of abuses in Saudi Arabia, currently being studied under the private, "confidential procedures" mechanism of the 53-member Commission, merit closer scrutiny by a U.N. independent expert, Howen said.
"Saudi Arabia is being protected by its security allies including the United States. We need to see the appointment of a (U.N.) expert for Saudi Arabia."
On Turkey, Amnesty said that it had avoided international scrutiny through solidarity with other Western countries, despite documented cases of torture and other abuses against Kurds.
"Turkey has powerful friends protecting their regional ally, a member of NATO and a buffer state against perceived Islamic threat," Howen said.
At this year's six-week Commission, Amnesty is focusing on Algeria, Colombia, Indonesia and East Timor, Nigeria and Turkey.
"These are five that are being ignored in particular," Howen said. "We will also to continue work intensively on the Great Lakes countries and China."
On China, Howen said: "We want real changes, but see diplomatic changes...We also see ambiguities creeping into the legal structure in Hong Kong."
An Amnesty spokesman, Mark Ogle, said the organisation was "pessimistic" about a resolution on China being adopted.
In Algeria, at least 50,000 have been killed by security forces and armed opposition groups during five years of violence, the rights group said.
Amnesty strongly condemned attacks by armed Islamic groups, including those on individuals and random killings by bomb explosions and repeated its call to end abuses.

"However, no level of violence by armed opposition groups, no matter how serious, can ever justify the Algerian security forces' recourse to extrajudicial executions, torture and 'disappearances'," Amnesty said.
The human rights situation in Colombia has worsened since the last annual U.N. session, according to Amnesty.
"Extrajudical executions, 'disappearances' and torture carried out by members of the security forces and their paramilitary allies have persisted and, in some areas, increased dramatically," it said.

Amnesty called on Indonesia to halt its "crackdown" on non-violent, political, human rights, labour and other activists. It urged Jakarta to address violations in East Timor and allow groups including Amnesty access to the area.

Indonesia has yet to identify those killed during, or account for those missing after, the 1991 massacre in Dili, "where at least 100 and possibly as many as 270 civilians" were killed when troops fired on a peaceful demonstration", it said.
Nigeria's current military government has a record of open contempt for human rights, including arbitrary detentions, unfair trials and extrajudicial executions, according to Amnesty.
